t.gola south@7.4,-11.2:
At the eastern edge of Sierra Leone, on the border with Liberia, there is one of the last big tracts of rainforest in West Africa. The Gola forest, which is split into several blocks, is part of the Upper Guinean forest, a hotspot of biodiversity, and its trees tower up to fifty metres, forming a dense canopy that blocks out the sun. It is home to the pygmy hippopotamus, a shy, forest-dwelling relative of the river hippo, the western chimpanzee, the Diana monkey, the red colobus, the forest elephant and the white-breasted guineafowl, and it has an astonishing array of birds, butterflies and frogs. Gola Rainforest National Park was created in 2011 to protect it.

The forest has a human story too. The villages around the edge are home to the Mende and Gola peoples, who have long lived from farming, hunting and gathering forest products. In the civil war from 1991 to 2002, the area was a battlefield, and logging and mining added to the destruction. Since the war, conservation groups and local communities have worked together to protect the forest, and income from ecotourism and cocoa farming on the fringes helps to give people a reason to keep it standing.

Reaching it is an adventure. Roads in this part of Sierra Leone are a mix of tarmac, laterite and mud, and in the rainy season, from May to October, many are impassable to all but the toughest vehicles. The dry season, from December to April, is the only sensible time, and even then you can expect rough tracks, river crossings on makeshift bridges, and sections of loose gravel. Gorahun and Zimmi, each with about four or five thousand people, are the nearest towns, but they offer only basic shops and the fuel may be sold from bottles at the roadside, so bring a spare can and a filter. Kenema, to the north-west, is the biggest regional town.

Expect heat, humidity and insects, and take malaria precautions. Local people are warm and curious, and a polite greeting goes a long way. Arrange access and guides through the park authorities, since the forest is dense and easy to get lost in.
t.peucang island@-6.7,105.3:
Peucang lies off the northwest tip of Java, a small island of white sand and thick forest on the edge of Ujung Kulon National Park, the last wild corner of that crowded island. Ujung Kulon is a peninsula whose coast was swept by the Krakatau tsunami of 1883, which emptied it of people and let the forest take over, and it is the last home of the Javan rhinoceros, one of the rarest large mammals on earth. The animals are shy and live in the dense lowland forest on the mainland, so you are very unlikely to see one, but the park also holds banteng wild cattle, deer, gibbons, macaques, wild boar and crocodiles.

There is no road to the island, so your ride ends on the mainland, and the usual route is from Labuan or Carita on the west coast of Banten, then south along a coastal road through villages, rice fields and coconut groves toward Sumur and the park gate at Tamanjaya. The road gets narrower and more broken as you go, with potholes, buses, motorbike taxis and chickens, and heavy rain brings mud and standing water. Distances take longer than you expect. From the end of the road you go by boat, a couple of hours across a sea that can be rough, with tourist boats booked through the park office or a guide.

On the island itself, the sand is white and the water is clear, with coral just offshore, and monitor lizards patrol the beach looking for scraps. Rusa deer graze on the lawn near the old guesthouse, which dates from a Dutch era, and long-tailed macaques raid anything left open. Walk quietly and you may hear hornbills in the canopy. The sea is warm all year, but the dry season, from about May to September, gives the calmest crossings and the clearest skies. Monsoon months can cancel boats.

Bring cash, since there are no machines, and take drinking water and insect repellent, since mosquitoes are a real concern. Permits for the park are needed and should be arranged ahead, ideally through an authorised operator, and rules change, so ask locally before relying on any detail.
t.pits of terracotta army@34.4,109.3:
In 1974 a group of farmers digging a well near the town of Lintong in Shaanxi struck something hard, and so began one of the great archaeological finds of the twentieth century. Below the farmland lay the Terracotta Army, thousands of life-size clay soldiers, horses and chariots, buried to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the man who unified China in 221 BC and became its first emperor. He ordered the burial complex to be started when he came to the throne, and tens of thousands of workers laboured on it for decades.

Three main pits have been opened. The largest holds an army in battle formation, with infantry, archers, cavalry and chariots, and each figure has distinct features, hairstyles and expressions, as if drawn from real soldiers. Originally they were painted in bright colours, and traces of pigment fade quickly on exposure to air, which is why excavation is slow and careful. Estimates suggest that there may be around eight thousand figures in total. The emperor's tomb mound itself, a short distance away, has not been opened, and ancient historians wrote that it contains rivers of mercury, which modern soil tests have partly supported.

Lintong is a small city set among pomegranate and persimmon orchards, and the nearby hot springs at Huaqing, where Tang emperors bathed, make a good extra stop. The ride from Xi'an is about forty kilometres, on busy roads that run through a flat plain with the Qin Mountains on the horizon. Go as early as you can, as tour buses fill the car park by mid-morning, and summer heat is fierce. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Chinese motorbike rules for foreigners are strict, so confirm permits ahead of time.

Lintong has fuel stations, restaurants and hotels, and Weinan, further east, is larger. Try roujiamo, a spiced pork sandwich, and biangbiang noodles, wide hand-pulled noodles from Shaanxi, and buy pomegranates in season. Allow at least half a day at the site, plus time for the museum, and bring water.
t.small wild goose pagoda@34.2,108.9:
Xi'an was Chang'an, the capital of the Tang dynasty and the eastern end of the Silk Road, and the Small Wild Goose Pagoda is one of the survivors from that golden age. It was built between about 707 and 709 to house Buddhist scriptures brought back from India by the monk Yijing, who travelled by sea and returned with hundreds of texts. It stands in the grounds of the Jianfu Temple, in a quiet garden just south of the city walls, a slim, tapering tower of brick with fifteen tiers of narrow eaves.

Its history is dramatic. A great earthquake in 1556 split the tower from top to bottom, and the upper levels were lost, so that it now has thirteen storeys. Later quakes closed the crack again, and the tower is said to have healed itself, a legend that locals enjoy. Its larger sibling, the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, built in 652 for the monk Xuanzang, lies a couple of kilometres to the south. A huge iron bell nearby is rung at certain times, with a deep note that is said to be heard across the city.

Xi'an is among the great historical cities of China, with its intact Ming city wall, which is about fourteen kilometres around and can be walked or cycled, the Bell and Drum Towers, and the Muslim Quarter, with its crowded lanes of street food. Traffic is heavy in the city centre, with many scooters and buses, so it is more comfortable to see the sights on foot or by bicycle. Spring and autumn offer the best weather, while summer is hot and winter cold and dry.

Xi'an has plenty of fuel, workshops and hotels, and the area around the pagoda has cafes and shops. Try a bowl of yangrou paomo, a lamb soup with crumbled flatbread, in the Muslim Quarter, and wander the garden at the temple in the early morning when it is quiet. Check requirements for foreign motorcyclists in China before you plan to ride.
t.site of weiyang palace in chang an city:
Weiyang Palace was the largest palace of the Han dynasty, and its ruins lie on the north-western edge of modern Xi'an in a flat expanse of fields and low earth mounds. Built in the early years of the Han, around two hundred years before the Common Era, under the chancellor Xiao He, the palace lay at the heart of the capital Chang'an and served as the seat of government for most of the Western Han and later dynasties. The site is reputed to be about six times the area of the Forbidden City in Beijing, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Silk Roads network that began at Chang'an and ran west across Asia.

Chang'an in the Han period was one of the two largest cities in the world, comparable with Rome, and the trade that flowed out of it carried silk, lacquer, bronze and tea westward, while horses, grapes, glass and ideas came back. Zhang Qian, the envoy who travelled west on the orders of the emperor, brought back the first reliable reports of Central Asia. At Weiyang there is little left to see in the way of walls and halls, only rammed-earth foundations, a few reconstructed gate sites and a museum, but the scale is impressive, and there is a kind of austere pleasure in standing in a vast empty field and knowing that it was once the centre of an empire.

Xi'an is a rich place to visit by other means. The Terracotta Army lies east of the city, the Ming city wall can be walked or cycled in an afternoon, and the Muslim Quarter fills each evening with grills, sweet shops and the smell of cumin and charcoal. Eat biangbiang noodles, wide hand-pulled ribbons in chilli oil, or a roujiamo, a stuffed bun of braised pork, and drink a small glass of sour plum juice.

Riding is limited to the city and its surroundings. Foreign riders in China need local permits and often a guide, so check carefully, and traffic in Xi'an is dense, with taxis, buses and electric scooters filling every lane. South of the city the Qinling mountains rise steeply, and the roads into them are among the best in the region, with tunnels and hairpins. Fuel stations are everywhere in the city. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, because summers are hot and humid, and winters are cold and grey.
t.waypoint 3@65.3,-14.4:
Egilsstaðir is the main town of east Iceland, set at the head of Lagarfljót, a long, dark glacial lake, with the Fljótsdalshérað plain spreading around it. For anyone riding the Ring Road around the island, it comes as a pleasant change after the empty highlands of the northeast, because suddenly there are trees. Iceland's largest forest, Hallormsstaðaskógur, grows along the lake's eastern shore, and the town has shops, a swimming pool and a handful of cafes.

The road here, Route 1, crosses the high plateau from Mývatn before descending into the valley, and it can be a harsh stretch. Wind is the main hazard. Gusts across the open ground can be strong enough to push a heavily loaded bike sideways, and fog and rain can reduce visibility quickly. Surfaces are generally good tarmac, but gravel sections and sudden changes can appear, and frost is possible outside summer. The best season for riding is roughly June to August, when the roads are clear and the days are very long.

Local legend adds a bit of colour. Lagarfljót is said to hold a serpent-like creature, the Lagarfljótsormur, and sightings have been reported for centuries. Whether you believe it or not, the lake has a calm, deep stillness that suits the story. From the town you can also drive toward the fjords to the east, with Seyðisfjörður, a steep-sided fjord with a ferry link to Europe, reached by a dramatic pass.

Fuel is not a concern here. Egilsstaðir, with its population of a couple of thousand, has stations, and the next ones toward the coast are at Reyðarfjörður and Eskifjörður, about thirty kilometres away, so fill up if you are heading to the fjords. In the empty stretches across the highlands, stations are far apart, so never let the tank fall below half.

This is a good place to rest, eat properly and check the forecast before the next leg. After the bare plateaus, the green valley and the calm lake feel almost gentle.
t.khuzhir@53.2,107.3:
Khuzhir is the one real village on Olkhon, the biggest island in Lake Baikal, a long, wind-scoured strip of steppe and pine forest about seventy kilometres long, lying close to the western shore. Baikal is the deepest lake on Earth, over sixteen hundred metres at its greatest depth, and holds about a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh water. It is also very old, perhaps twenty-five million years, and its waters are astonishingly clear, so that you can see stones many metres down in summer.

The island is the centre of the Buryat shamanic tradition, and the rocky headland just outside Khuzhir, Shaman Rock, is a sacred place with colourful ribbons tied on posts. Sunsets here, with the light turning the water gold and the cliffs red, draw crowds in summer. Seals, the Baikal nerpa, live in the lake, and eagles and gulls ride the wind. The island's roads are mostly sandy and unpaved, and the main way of getting around is by old Soviet vans, which bounce over the ruts in clouds of dust.

Getting here is part of the trip. A ferry runs across the narrow strait, the Olkhon Gate, from the mainland near Sakhyurta, and queues for it can be long in summer, when everyone wants to cross at once. Ferries sometimes stop when ice is forming or breaking, so check the schedule. For riders, the riding on the island is a test, with soft sand, corrugations and washouts, and heavy bikes can be tricky. A trail leads north to Cape Khoboy, the island's northern tip, with big views over open water.

Khuzhir has just over a thousand people, with guesthouses, cafes and small shops, and fish from the lake, especially smoked omul, is the local treat. Fuel is sold in the village, but supplies can be limited, so fill up on the mainland before crossing. Summer is short and bright, with cool nights, and in winter the lake freezes so thickly that cars drive across it. Foreign riders should check current conditions and rules before planning travel.
t.ust barguzin@53.4,109.0:
Ust-Barguzin sits where the Barguzin River spills into Lake Baikal on its eastern shore, a long way from the crowds on the west side. The valley behind it is wide and flat, with the Barguzin Range rising on one side and the lake on the other, and the Barguzin wind, a strong gale that blows down the valley, is known to sailors and fishermen across the lake. The Barguzin Nature Reserve, founded in 1916 to protect the sable, is the oldest in Russia, and its forests are home to bears, elk and deer.

The town has about seven thousand people and a remote feel, with wooden houses, fishing boats and a harbour. Buryat and Russian culture mix here, and the area is known for smoked omul, the lake's silvery fish. Hot springs bubble up along the shore at places such as Goryachinsk, to the south, and a few of them have simple bathhouses where you can soak after a day on the road. Across Barguzin Bay, the Svyatoy Nos peninsula is a wild, mountainous headland that is part of the Zabaikalsky National Park, with views over the lake.

The riding from Ulan-Ude is long and unhurried. The road runs east, then north along the broad valley, with steppe, forest and lines of mountains in the distance, and the surface is mostly asphalt with patches of rough pavement. Some side tracks are gravel or sand. Weather can change fast on the lake, with cold wind and rain in the summer, and mosquitoes and horseflies in July are fierce. The best months are late June to early September.

Fuel, food and rooms are available in Ust-Barguzin, but supplies can run short in summer, so fill up when you can. Villages along the valley are small and far apart. A walk on the sandy shore at sunset, with the wind dropping and the lake going still, is a fine way to end a day. Foreign riders should check current conditions and rules before planning travel.
t.can tho@10.0,105.8:
Can Tho is the capital of the Mekong Delta, a flat green country of rivers, canals and orchards that is built by water and travels by water. The city sits on the Hau River, one of the big distributaries of the Mekong, and its riverfront at Ninh Kieu is the place where people stroll in the evening, eat, and watch the boats. The real show is at dawn, when the floating market at Cai Rang gathers boats loaded with pineapples, watermelons and sweet potatoes, each with a sample of its cargo hung on a pole at the bow so that buyers can see what is for sale from a distance.

This is a landscape you ride rather than conquer. The delta has little elevation, and its roads follow the canals and dykes, running straight past rice fields, coconut palms and fruit orchards, with the odd concrete bridge or narrow footbridge made of bamboo, the famous monkey bridges. Side roads and village lanes are paved but narrow, so you share them with scooters, bicycles and the occasional buffalo. Schoolchildren on bikes pass in white uniforms, and houses are built on stilts or with a boat tied to the front step. The pleasure is in the pace and the endless detail.

Weather is hot and humid all year, and the rainy season, from May to November, brings heavy afternoon downpours that turn the roads slick and flood low sections. The best time to ride is the dry season, from December to April, when the sky is blue, the breeze is dry and the fruit is at its best. Start early to avoid the midday heat, and carry plenty of water.

Can Tho has all the fuel and food you need, with stations along every main road and street stalls serving noodles, grilled fish and the local specialities, including rice-paper rolls and fish cooked in clay pots. Beyond the city the roads are quiet but fuel is less frequent, so keep an eye on the gauge. It is easy to take a wrong turn among the canals and end up on a ferry landing or a dead-end bridge, which is part of the charm, as long as you have the time.
t.seydisfjordur@65.3,-14.0:
Seyðisfjörður lies at the end of a long, narrow fjord in the east of Iceland, hemmed in by steep mountains and cut off from the rest of the country by a high pass that closes with the first serious snow. That isolation has shaped it. In the late nineteenth century it was one of the richest towns in Iceland, a herring port with Norwegian merchants who built tall wooden houses in a style found nowhere else on the island, and in 1906 the first telegraph cable from Europe came ashore here. The old buildings survive, painted in cheerful colours, and give the place the air of a small Norwegian port that has wandered a long way west.

To get here you climb from Egilsstaðir over Fjarðarheiði, a mountain road that rises to about six hundred metres through moorland and often through cloud, then drops in a series of bends towards the sea with waterfalls tumbling beside the tarmac. It is a short but rewarding ride, tight in places, with the views opening suddenly as you come off the plateau. Fog and snow can arrive in any season outside high summer, so check the forecast. Ice can linger on the shadowed corners well into spring.

In the town, the famous sight is a small blue wooden church at the end of a street painted with a rainbow path, and the place is full of artists, designers and a lively summer festival. A technical museum, a few galleries and good cafes make it an easy afternoon. The ferry from Denmark and the Faroe Islands docks here, so you will often see motorcycles with foreign plates unloading, riders looking slightly dazed after the long sea crossing. Mountains such as Bjólfur rise straight from the water behind the houses, and in 2020 a large landslide damaged part of the town, a reminder of how steep the surroundings are.

Fuel is available in the town, as are shops, a bakery and several places to eat, with fresh fish a safe order. Egilsstaðir, roughly eighteen kilometres back over the pass, has the larger supermarkets and more services. Accommodation fills up around ferry days and festival time, so book ahead in summer.

The best time to come is late afternoon or evening, when the low sun lights the fjord and the colours on the houses glow. Keep a warm layer to hand, because the air coming off the water has a sharp edge even in July.
t.buon ma thuot@12.7,108.1:
Buôn Ma Thuột is the coffee capital of Vietnam, and you can smell it before you see it. The city sits on the red basalt plateau of the Central Highlands, at around five hundred metres, where volcanic soil and a distinct dry season suit robusta better than almost anywhere in the world. Vietnam is the second-largest coffee producer on earth, and this province, Đắk Lắk, grows a big share of it. In the cafés, the coffee comes in a small steel filter that drips slowly into a glass, thick, bitter and sweet with condensed milk. Order it, sit on a plastic stool, and let the street move around you.

The name comes from the Ê Đê people, the indigenous community that has lived in the highlands for centuries in long stilt houses, and elephants were once a major part of the local economy. Today, a few remain in the villages and national park nearby, and responsible tourism has moved away from riding them. There is a coffee museum in the city with a good collection of history and equipment, and the waterfalls at Dray Nur and Dray Sáp lie a short ride to the southwest, wide and noisy after the rains.

History arrives bluntly here. In March 1975, North Vietnamese forces attacked Buôn Ma Thuột, taking the city after a short fight and starting the offensive that ended the war within two months. A tank stands as a monument in the city today. The Hồ Chí Minh Road, once a secret supply line through the mountains, runs through the highlands and has been rebuilt as a modern highway, and following it from the north brings you through forest, rubber plantations and farm country to arrive here.

The riding on the plateau is generally easy, but demanding in its own way: trucks, buses, scooters, dogs and pedestrians all share the road, and you should expect surprises. Surfaces are mostly decent, with occasional potholes after the rains. The dry season, from about November to April, is the sensible time, with cool nights and clear skies. The wet season brings afternoon downpours.

Fuel is easy in a city of this size, and you will find pumps on all main roads. Food is cheap and excellent, with bún, grilled meat and pho on every corner. Finish the ride with a long coffee.
t.bayandai@53.1,105.5:
Bayandai is a Buryat village of just under three thousand people on the dry, open land west of Baikal, a region of rolling steppe where the Irkutsk basin begins to fold into the hills before the lake. This is the homeland of the Ust-Orda Buryats, a branch of the Mongol-speaking peoples who have herded cattle and horses here for centuries, and the district takes its name from the village. You notice it in the details: the signs written in two scripts, the sacred groves on the hills, and the little posts decorated with coloured ribbons where people leave offerings for the spirits of the place.

On a ride from Irkutsk towards the Olkhon ferry, Bayandai is one of the useful markers along the way. The road here is open and fast, with long straights and gentle rises through grassland and scattered pines. Traffic is moderate but includes lorries and the occasional tourist minibus, and the surface can be rough in places where heavy vehicles have worn grooves into the asphalt. Summer is dry and often windy, and the sunsets across the steppe are some of the best you will find in this part of Siberia. Spring can bring bare, brown hills before the grass turns green in late May.

With a population in the thousands, the village has shops, simple cafes and a petrol station or two, though you should not count on late opening hours or on every pump being in use. Larger towns in the area are far away, so it is wise to fill up here rather than trust that the next village will have something. Try buuz, the steamed Buryat dumplings filled with meat, and the milk tea that comes with salt and sometimes butter, a taste that surprises visitors but suits the climate.

There is also history in the ground. The steppe here is dotted with ancient burial mounds and stone circles from peoples who lived long before the Buryats arrived, and the wider Baikal region has been a crossroads for centuries. A short walk beyond the last houses is often enough to find a quiet knoll with a view across a landscape that feels both very large and very old. Then it is back on the bike, with the ferry and the island still ahead.
t.khoboy cape@53.4,107.8:
Cape Khoboy is where Olkhon Island runs out of land. It marks the northern tip of the largest island in Lake Baikal, a long finger of rock and steppe that lies parallel to the western shore, and the cape ends in cliffs of dark stone pierced by narrow caves, with the open water of the lake stretching off towards the far mountains. The nearest village is Khuzhir, thirty-eight kilometres to the south, and between the two there is almost nothing built. That emptiness is exactly why people come.

The ride is an adventure rather than a road. From Khuzhir a track leads north across the island, sandy in places, rutted in others, and best handled on a bike you are comfortable picking up. Gradients are gentle but the surface changes constantly, with hard-packed gravel, soft sand patches, and corrugations that can shake the fillings out of your teeth if you hit them at the wrong speed. Rain turns clay to grease, and the wind that comes across Baikal is sharp and persistent, so dress for cold even on a warm day.

The land you ride across is unusual: dry steppe with feather grass and wild thyme, interrupted by patches of pine and larch, and the smell is dry and herbal, nothing like the damp forests of the western shore. Olkhon is sacred ground for Buryat shamans, and the rock called Shamanka near Khuzhir is the best known of many holy places on the island. At the cape, as elsewhere, you will see coloured ribbons tied to posts, and visitors are expected to show a little reverence rather than treating the place as a playground.

Time your visit for late afternoon, when the light on the cliffs turns amber and the lake takes on a deep indigo. Baikal's seals, the nerpa, haul out on rocks in some seasons, though you are more likely to see gulls and cormorants. Bring food and water for the day, take your time on the track, and remember that help is a long way off if something goes wrong.
t.barguzin@53.6,109.6:
The Barguzin Valley is one of those places that gets its identity from being closed in on both sides. A long, flat basin runs for around two hundred kilometres between the Barguzin range, which separates it from the eastern shore of Baikal, and the Ikat range on the other side, and the river that gives the valley its name winds along the middle before reaching the lake. The town of Barguzin, with roughly six thousand people, is one of the oldest Russian settlements in the region, begun as a fortified outpost in the middle of the seventeenth century, and the older streets still carry a faint trace of that frontier past.

Riding into the valley feels like entering a separate world. The road is mostly straight and open, with views of the snow-streaked ridges on one side and fields of grass and wildflowers on the other. In summer the meadows are bright with colour, and cattle graze right up to the road, so keep an eye out for animals. The surface is a mix of reasonable asphalt and rougher stretches, and distances between villages are long. Fuel is available in the town, but not everywhere along the valley, so treat it as the place to fill up before pushing on.

The Barguzin range holds the Barguzin Nature Reserve, which is often described as the oldest in Russia, founded in 1916 to protect the sable. The mountains behind it are a wilderness of cedar forest and bare ridges, home to brown bears, elk and the sable that gave the reserve its purpose. You will not ride into it, but you feel it in the air and in the shape of the horizon. A cold wind named after the valley, the barguzin, blows down toward the lake and can turn a calm morning into a rough crossing for boats.

Local food is simple and filling: omul from Baikal, smoked or salted, and the warm dumplings that appear on every table. If you can, take an hour to wander the town and watch the daily routine, because Barguzin is not a museum but a living place where people still move to the rhythm of the seasons. Late June to early September is the best window, with long days and mild nights.
t.kyakhta@50.4,106.5:
Kyakhta once made the world's tea trade turn. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries this border town, wedged against Mongolia, was the point where Russian furs and goods were exchanged for Chinese tea carried north by camel caravan, and the merchants who grew rich on it built stone houses, a cathedral and a reputation that reached Moscow. The Treaty of Kyakhta in 1727 fixed the frontier and formalised the trade, which is why the road from Ulan-Ude is still called the Tea Road. Around eighteen thousand people live here now, and the old merchant district retains a faded grandeur beside the newer, plainer streets.

The ride from Ulan-Ude follows the Selenga valley south for a couple of hundred kilometres, and it is a comfortable, honest piece of Siberian road. The highway is mostly good asphalt with long straights, easy bends and occasional patches of rough surface. Traffic is steady, with lorries heading to the border, so overtaking needs patience. The landscape opens into dry steppe and low hills, with herds of sheep and the odd Buddhist stupa beside the road. Summers are hot and dry, winters brutally cold, and May and September give the best balance of light and comfort.

Because it is a frontier town, Kyakhta lies within a border zone, so carry your passport and be ready for checks on the approach. Fuel and food are easy to find, with several stations and cafes, and the town is a sensible place to refill and eat before the return leg. Altanbulag on the Mongolian side is only a few kilometres away, and Sükhbaatar, the larger Mongolian town, a little farther, but you cannot simply wander across without the proper paperwork.

Take an hour to look at the old town. The Resurrection Cathedral, a big merchant church that has survived some hard decades, and the local museum, which tells the story of the trade, are the best ways to understand why a small place in the steppe mattered so much. The wind often carries the dry smell of grass and dust across the streets, and the sky is huge. It is a town that has lost its money but kept its pride.
t.xingjiaosi pagodas@34.1,109.0:
When the monk Xuanzang returned to Chang'an in the seventh century after sixteen years of travel to India, he brought back hundreds of Buddhist scriptures, which he spent the rest of his life translating, and his journey later inspired the classic novel Journey to the West, with its Monkey King. After his death in 664, his remains were buried at Xingjiao Temple, on the slopes south of the city, and a five-storey brick pagoda was built over them in 669. Next to it stand two smaller pagodas for two of his disciples. The three pagodas, in a peaceful temple setting, are part of the Silk Roads World Heritage site, a tribute to one of the most famous travellers along that route.

The temple sits on a terrace overlooking the Fan river valley, with the Qinling mountains, the Zhongnan range, rising to the south. The area is less visited than the big sites in the city, and the atmosphere is calm, with monks, incense and the sound of bells. Xi'an, the modern city that grew on the site of Chang'an, the capital of the Tang dynasty and starting point of the Silk Road, is about twenty kilometres to the north, with its city walls, the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, also linked to Xuanzang, and the Muslim quarter.

The Qinling mountains are the great natural divide of China, separating the dry north from the humid south, and their forests are home to giant pandas, golden monkeys and takins. Roads lead south from the plain into the mountains through narrow valleys and over passes, with plenty of bends and fine scenery, though the traffic can be heavy at weekends. Remember that riding in China as a foreigner requires a Chinese licence and registered vehicle, that many cities restrict motorcycles in their central areas, and that expressways are usually closed to them.

There are small shops and restaurants near the temple, and Xi'an has everything you could need. The food of Xi'an is famous: roujiamo, a kind of Chinese burger of stewed meat in flatbread; biangbiang noodles, wide hand-pulled noodles with chilli oil; and yangrou paomo, bread soaked in mutton soup. To the east of the city, near Lintong, lies the Terracotta Army of the first emperor of China, one of the greatest archaeological finds of the twentieth century.
t.honje nature reserve@-6.7,105.6:
Nobody takes a motorcycle into the interior of Ujung Kulon, because there is no road to take it on. The park fills the far western tip of Java, a peninsula where the island simply runs out into the Sunda Strait, and Honje is its eastern block, a hilly, forested reserve of lowland rainforest and mangrove that is the first part you reach from the mainland. Beyond it lie the lowlands, the Peucang islands, and Gunung Payung, and the roads stop at the villages on the edge.

The park's fame rests on the Javan rhinoceros, one of the rarest large mammals on earth, and the last viable population lives here, very shy and rarely seen by anyone. The forest also holds banteng, Javan gibbons, leopards, mouse deer, and an enormous number of birds, and the peninsula was left to nature in part because of what happened in 1883. The eruption of Krakatau, whose island sits out in the strait and is part of the same wider area, sent a tsunami that swept over this coast, killed tens of thousands of people on both sides of the strait, and emptied the shore. The forest grew back over the old settlements, which is one reason the park exists.

The ride, then, is the approach. From the west Javan coastal towns the roads run along the sea, hot, humid and busy with trucks, scooters and goats, and the surface changes quickly from good asphalt to broken patches. Distances look short on the map and take much longer than expected, so leave early and plan for rain, which can arrive in a few minutes during the wet season. Dry months, roughly May to September, are kinder to a rider and to anyone planning a boat trip.

Entry to the park requires a permit and usually a local guide, and the rangers will tell you what is open, so ask before you go rather than turn up and hope.
t.site of daming palace in chang an city o:
At its height in the seventh and eighth centuries, Chang'an, the Tang capital, was probably the biggest city in the world, with a population of around a million and a street plan so precise that Japan copied it for Kyoto and Nara. At the north of the city, on a plateau above the rest, stood the Daming Palace, the imperial residence from the 630s, with a great audience hall, the Hanyuan Hall, set on a raised platform, from which the emperor looked out over the city. It was the political heart of the empire, and a place of ceremony, intrigue and banquets, receiving envoys from Persia, Japan, Korea and Central Asia.

Today nothing stands but earth platforms and foundations, which have been preserved in a large archaeological park with a museum, and the site gives a sense of scale, since the palace area was several times the size of the Forbidden City in Beijing. UNESCO listed it in 2014 as part of the Silk Roads, and it is a quiet counterpoint to the crowds at the Terracotta Army, which is about thirty-five kilometres east, in a different era, and which also forms part of the picture of ancient Shaanxi.

Xi'an is a big, busy city of several million, and riding in it means dense traffic, electric scooters, and crowded intersections. The Ming-era city walls, which are still intact, can be cycled on top, and the Muslim Quarter near the Drum Tower is a maze of lanes with food stalls. Away from the city, the Qinling mountains to the south have good roads with long climbs and bends, and the sacred mountain of Huashan is a few hours to the east. Winters are cold and dry, summers hot and humid, and the best seasons are spring and autumn.

Fuel and food are plentiful, and Xi'an is famous for its noodles, especially the wide, hand-pulled biangbiang noodles, for roujiamo, a pork-filled flatbread, and for a stew of lamb and bread called yangrou paomo. The park is large, so wear comfortable shoes and bring a hat, and allow time for the museum, which explains the buildings that are no longer there.
t.panaitan island@-6.6,105.2:
There are no roads on Panaitan Island, and you will not reach it by motorcycle, so this stop is one to read about before you ride to the coast and board a boat. It lies off the south-western tip of Java, a few kilometres from the mainland, within the Ujung Kulon National Park, one of the last great stretches of lowland rainforest on the island, and the nearest road ends at small villages on the peninsula's edge, such as Sumur and Tamanjaya.

The park is a refuge for the Javan rhinoceros, one of the rarest large mammals on earth, with fewer than a hundred animals left, all living on the mainland peninsula. Banteng wild cattle, rusa deer, leopards, gibbons, and sea turtles that nest on the beaches share the forest. On Panaitan itself you will find macaques, mouse deer, monitor lizards and thick jungle, along with reefs, white sand beaches and one of the best-known surf breaks in Indonesia. A weathered Hindu statue, left from some earlier culture, stands on the hill, a reminder that Java's religious history was layered long before Islam arrived.

The area is also a place of geological violence. Krakatau, whose 1883 eruption was one of the loudest events ever recorded, lies in the strait to the north-east, and the great waves from that eruption killed tens of thousands of people along the coasts of Java and Sumatra, and wrecked the forests of Ujung Kulon. The new volcano, Anak Krakatau, collapsed in December 2018 and sent another tsunami onto these shores. For that reason, the coast has a feeling of being at the edge of something.

The roads that lead there are the best part for a rider. From Serang the route goes through Pandeglang to Labuan on the west coast, where the highway is busy with trucks and minibuses, and then along the coast to Sumur, with a mix of potholes, bends and views of the Sunda Strait. Traffic thins out beyond Labuan. Rain falls most of the year, and the dry season, from May to September, is the safest time for the sea crossing, since boats do not run in rough water. Access to the park requires a permit and a guide, arranged in advance, so plan carefully.

Fuel is the main practical point. Buy it in Labuan or Pandeglang, because stations are rare on the peninsula and only roadside bottles are available in the villages. Mosquitoes are fierce, so cover up.
t.ujung kulon national park@-6.7,105.3:
Ujung Kulon sits at the far western tip of Java, a peninsula that points out into the Sunda Strait like a thumb, and it is the last refuge of the Javan rhinoceros. A few dozen of these shy, armoured animals survive, the rarest large mammals on earth, and the whole of the world's population lives in this one forest. The park was protected in the early twentieth century, partly because the great eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 had devastated the coast and left the area empty of people, and the forest recovered. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage site in 1991.

The country is lowland rainforest, mangrove and swamp, with long beaches of pale sand, coral reefs offshore and islands like Peucang, which have clear water and sea turtles. The forest holds banteng wild cattle, Javan gibbons, leopards, monitor lizards and a huge range of birds. Rhinos are almost never seen, which is part of their survival, and visitors usually go to see the other wildlife and the scenery. The air is hot and damp, with the smell of leaf mould and salt. Krakatoa, and its child, Anak Krakatau, lie across the strait, and in 2018 a collapse of the young volcano caused a tsunami that struck the coast here and in nearby Banten.

Reaching the park is a journey. The roads from Jakarta run through busy towns and then dwindle as they approach the peninsula, passing through villages of fishermen and farmers, with palm groves, rice fields and small shops. Surfaces can be rough, traffic is a mix of trucks, motorbikes and animals, and rain turns parts of the road to mud. The approach to the park is by permit, with a boat needed for the islands, and conditions vary, so ask a local operator.

This is remote country with no real town close by. Fuel and supplies should be bought in larger towns such as Labuan or Pandeglang before you head west, and petrol is often sold in bottles by roadside stalls. The dry season, from May to September, is the best time, and the rains of the monsoon can make the roads and the boat crossings difficult.
t.gola central@7.7,-10.9:
Gola is the last big block of the Upper Guinean rainforest in Sierra Leone, and the central part of it lies close to the border with Liberia in the south-east of the country. Sierra Leone made it a national park in 2011, after decades of logging and the shock of a civil war that ran from 1991 to 2002, and it is run with the help of local communities, who receive a share of the benefits and who have a role in protecting the trees. The forest is split into three main blocks, North, Central and South, and the centre is the heart of the system.

Under the canopy lives a rich community of animals, most of them hard to see. Pygmy hippos, small forest relatives of the river hippo, creep through the swamps at night. Chimpanzees, Diana monkeys, red colobus and forest elephants share the forest with a wide range of hornbills and other birds, and the white-necked rockfowl, a bizarre bald bird that nests on cave walls, is a prize for birdwatchers. Many of these species are rare elsewhere because their forest has been cut.

The atmosphere is wet and green, with the smell of leaf litter and the constant noise of insects, frogs and birds. Rain falls heavily from May to October, and the forest tracks turn to slippery mud, while the dry season from November to April is the time for visits, with a hot dusty haze known as the harmattan arriving in the middle of it. Mornings are the best time to hear the forest at its busiest, and the nights are loud with tree hyraxes and frogs.

Getting here means a long, slow journey. The main roads from Freetown to the east of the country have been improved in recent years, but the tracks leading to the villages near the park are laterite, rutted and sometimes impassable in the rains. A rider needs a robust bike, local advice and plenty of time, and a guide arranged through the park's community offices is worth the money. Jojoima and Giehun are small towns near the northern edge, and Daru, a bit larger, is to the south.

None of them can be counted on for a steady fuel supply, so fill the tank in the larger towns of Kenema or Bo and carry spares. Food in the villages is simple and filling, rice with cassava leaf or groundnut stew, and a visit is welcomed if you ask the chief first. Travel here is slow, but the reward is a forest that is still alive.
t.great wild goose pagoda@34.2,109.0:
The Great Wild Goose Pagoda rises seven storeys above the southern part of Xi'an, a plain, tapered tower of grey brick that has been leaning slightly for centuries. It was built in 652, in the Tang dynasty, to store the Buddhist scriptures that the monk Xuanzang brought back from India after a journey of seventeen years, returning to the capital Chang'an in 645. His travels, over deserts, mountains and kingdoms, inspired the famous sixteenth-century novel Journey to the West, with its Monkey King, one of the best-loved stories in Chinese literature. In the temple of Da Ci'en that surrounds the pagoda, Xuanzang worked with a team of translators for the rest of his life.

The pagoda is about sixty-four metres high today, and you can climb the stairs inside to look out over the city. Around it lies a lively square, with a fountain show in the evenings that is said to be among the largest in Asia, and a calm temple compound with halls, bells and old trees. Nearby, the Xingjiaosi pagodas hold the remains of Xuanzang, and the site of the Weiyang Palace recalls the great Han capital. Chang'an was the eastern end of the Silk Road, among the largest cities in the world in its day, and the pagoda is a surviving piece of that golden age.

Xi'an is a city of more than six million, and the food is a pleasure: hand-pulled biangbiang noodles, roujiamo, a sort of Chinese hamburger with braised pork in flatbread, and lamb soup with crumbled bread, much of it in the Muslim quarter near the Drum Tower. The old city walls, among the best preserved in China, can be walked or cycled on top, and the evening light on the wall is lovely.

An honest note about riding: foreign visitors cannot simply bring a motorbike to China and ride around, since the country requires special permits, local registration and a guide for any foreign vehicle, and in many Chinese cities motorbikes are restricted in the centre. For most people, getting here means arriving by train or plane and enjoying the city on foot or by bicycle. Fuel is not an issue in a city of this size, and the roads in the countryside around Shaanxi are largely excellent. Spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons, as summers are hot and winters can be cold and smoggy. Check air quality before climbing the tower, since haze can hide the view.
t.mausoleum of the first qin emperor@34.4,:
Beneath a large, tree-covered mound at the foot of Mount Li, east of Xi'an, lies the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, who unified China in 221 BC and became its first emperor. He ruled for only eleven years more, dying in 210 BC, but in that time he standardised weights, measures, writing and the axle width of carts, linked the northern walls into an early Great Wall, and conscripted hundreds of thousands of labourers for his projects. The tomb mound, which still rises about fifty metres, has never been opened. The ancient historian Sima Qian wrote that the burial chamber held a model of the empire with rivers of mercury, and modern soil tests have found high levels of mercury around the mound.

What the world knows is the Terracotta Army. In 1974 farmers digging a well found fragments of clay figures, and archaeologists uncovered an astonishing army of thousands of life-size warriors, with horses and chariots, buried in pits about a kilometre and a half from the tomb to guard the emperor in the afterlife. Each figure has a different face, and many once carried real bronze weapons and were painted in bright colours, which have faded since they were exposed to the air. The site was listed by UNESCO in 1987, and excavation continues, with many figures yet to be uncovered.

The surrounding area is a farming country of pomegranate and persimmon orchards, and Lintong, the nearby town of about seventy-five thousand, is famous for its pomegranates, sold from roadside stalls in autumn. Close by are the hot springs at Huaqing Pool, a favourite retreat of Tang emperors, and the mountain where Chiang Kai-shek was arrested in 1936 in the Xi'an Incident. In the evenings, the town is lively, with night markets selling skewers, noodles and sweet persimmon cakes.

On the question of riding, foreign visitors need to know that travelling by motorbike in China is only possible with a complex set of permits, a local licence and normally a guide, so most arrive by train, coach or taxi from Xi'an, about thirty kilometres to the west. The roads in the area are modern, busy with coaches and trucks, and fuel is widely available. The site is crowded in summer and on public holidays, so go early in the morning or in the cooler months of April, May, October and November, and take time in the museum rather than rushing through the pits.
t.ujung kulon peninsula@-6.8,105.4:
The western tip of Java is a place where roads give up and the forest takes over. Ujung Kulon, the peninsula that pokes into the Sunda Strait, is a national park protecting the last wild population of the Javan rhinoceros, one of the rarest large mammals on Earth, along with banteng cattle, wild pigs, gibbons, langurs and a great diversity of birds. UNESCO listed it in 1991. Honje, on the mainland side, is a nature reserve of lowland rainforest, a green mass of tall trees, palms and tangled vines, where the air is thick, warm and loud with insects.

The coast here carries the scars of the region's volcanic history. In 1883 the eruption of Krakatoa, which lies just offshore, sent a tsunami surging across the strait, killing tens of thousands of people and sweeping through the lowlands of what is now the park. In December 2018, a collapse on the flank of its offspring, Anak Krakatau, triggered another tsunami that struck the coast of Banten without warning. The forest has since recovered, and the area feels both wild and fragile.

Getting here by motorcycle means riding the coastal roads of Banten, from towns such as Labuan toward Sumur, through villages, rice fields and coconut groves. The road surface can be uneven, with potholes and washouts after heavy rain, and traffic is a mix of motorbikes, minibuses and trucks. The weather is hot and humid, with a rainy season from roughly November to March. Check the conditions with local people before you set out, and carry plenty of water. There are no towns listed close to this point, so fuel is a practical concern: fill up in the last substantial town, and carry spare if you can, because roadside bottles of petrol are available but of variable quality.

Access to the park itself is controlled, with permits and guides required, and the rhinos are shy, so you will almost certainly not see one. The reward is in the forest and the sea, the sounds of birds at dawn and the sight of the coast from a boat. It is a remote, quiet and slightly mysterious place, and the effort of getting there is part of its character.
t.silk roads the routes network of chang a:
Chang'an, now Xi'an, was the eastern end of the Silk Road, and in the Tang dynasty it was probably the biggest city in the world, a grid of walled wards with a million people, Persian merchants, Sogdian horse traders, Japanese students and Buddhist pilgrims from India. This point is south of the modern city, at the Xingjiao Temple, where two small brick pagodas stand on a bluff over the Fan river. They hold the remains of Xuanzang, the monk who walked to India in the seventh century and came back after sixteen years with hundreds of scriptures, and of two of his disciples. His journey inspired the later novel Journey to the West, with its Monkey King, and the temple has a quiet, scholarly atmosphere.

The three pagodas are modest in size, the tallest of them about twenty metres, with rows of brick eaves and small windows, and they stand in a leafy compound with old cypress and pine trees. After the crowds at the Terracotta Army and the Big Wild Goose Pagoda, it is a relief. Beside the temple, a small hall shows the story, and monks go about their business, with incense and slow bells.

Riding in Xi'an is a different matter. The city is a vast grid of ring roads, traffic jams, electric scooters, taxis and buses, and the provincial and national rules about foreign vehicles make it hard for a visitor to ride in person. Most arrive by metro or a hired driver. The city wall, which is the Ming wall rebuilt on the Tang foundations, can be cycled on a rented bike in an afternoon, and the south gate at dusk, with the lights on the battlements, is wonderful. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, summer is hot and heavy, and winter is dry and cold, with smog some days.

Everything is within reach, since Xi'an has over six million people, and the Muslim Quarter is the place for food. Try the roujiamo, a stuffed bun filled with spiced lamb or pork, biangbiang noodles, which are broad and chewy, and the steamed lamb and bread soup called yangrou paomo. Fuel and repair shops are in the suburbs, as one would expect. Visit the temple in the morning, when it is calm, and check opening hours, which can change. Carry your passport for hotel check-ins and some tickets.
t.gola north@7.8,-10.7:
Forest this tall and this old is rare in West Africa now, and the Gola rainforest in eastern Sierra Leone is one of the largest pieces left of the Upper Guinean belt that once ran from Guinea to Ghana. Gola North is the northern block of the national park, which was formally established in 2011 and runs along the border with Liberia, where the forest continues into a matching protected area on the other side. It is a place where conservation has been built on top of a very hard recent history, because the civil war of 1991 to 2002 passed through this region and left deep scars.

The wildlife here is secretive. Western chimpanzees, Diana monkeys, forest elephants and pygmy hippos are all resident, and the white-necked picathartes, a bald-headed bird that builds mud nests on rock faces, is the species birdwatchers travel for. Most visitors will see far less than that: butterflies the size of saucers, hornbills crashing through the canopy, and the constant noise of insects and frogs. Under the trees the air is warm, wet and dark, and it smells of rot and flowers at the same time.

Riding here means laterite. The roads in the east of Sierra Leone are red earth, graded in the dry season and slick as grease in the rains, which run from May to October. December to March is the sensible time, though harmattan dust can fog the horizon. A dual-sport bike is the sensible choice, and river crossings may be simple wooden bridges or none at all.

The nearest place of any size is Jojoima, about sixteen kilometres off, with a population around three thousand. Do not count on reliable fuel there; Kenema, a large town farther west, is the realistic place to fill the tank, and a spare can is wise. They know the trails, and they know which bridges are safe.
t.egilsstadir@65.3,-14.4:
Egilsstaðir is the capital of east Iceland in the way a village can be a capital: it has a population of about two thousand, an airport, a supermarket, a swimming pool and a good reputation. It sits on the flat shore of Lagarfljót, a long glacial lake that stretches south-west for about twenty-five kilometres and is said to be home to a monster. The Lagarfljót worm has been reported since the Middle Ages, and a few years back a farmer even filmed something floating in the water, which the locals prefer to leave unexplained. The lake is murky grey-green with glacier silt, so a monster would have no trouble hiding.

You arrive here after a long and varied stretch of the Ring Road. From Jökulsárlón in the south-east, the route follows the coast through the East Fjords, past Höfn and Djúpivogur, through narrow tunnels, along cliffs and under steep, scree-covered mountains, before turning inland over mountain roads. The riding is remarkable: long straights beside the sea, winding climbs over passes, gravel-edged bends and distances that feel bigger than the numbers. The wind is the main danger, with gusts strong enough to move a loaded bike, and weather can change within an hour. Check forecasts and road conditions before setting off, and treat the warning signs seriously.

Egilsstaðir has everything a rider needs: fuel stations, supermarkets, cafés, a campsite, hotels and guesthouses, and it is the best place for supplies for miles in any direction. Fuel stations in smaller villages are limited, and some pumps are unmanned card-only machines, so carry a card with a pin. Nearby, the forest of Hallormsstaður is the largest in Iceland, a plantation and native birch woodland where you can walk among trees taller than a house, which for Iceland is a minor miracle.

From town you can ride over the steep pass of Fjarðarheiði to Seyðisfjörður, a colourful fjord village that looks like a postcard, with a ferry connection to Denmark. The road climbs to over 600 metres through switchbacks that can be foggy and snowy, and it is a rewarding ride on a clear day. The Vök Baths, floating hot pools on a nearby lake, give a good soak after a day's riding.

Food is simple: lamb soup, fresh fish, skyr and strong coffee. Summer is the main season, and in winter conditions can be severe.
t.kon tum@14.3,108.0:
Kon Tum is a small, quiet city in the Central Highlands of Vietnam, at about five hundred metres above sea level, where the Dak Bla River winds through a plateau of red earth, coffee, rubber and pepper. It is a place where the Vietnamese world meets the world of the highland peoples, the Bahnar, Sedang and Jarai among them, whose villages, longhouses and traditions still survive in the surrounding hills. The city is often overlooked in favour of busier places, which is part of its appeal.

The best-known landmark is the wooden church, built in the early twentieth century by French missionaries, a large timber building in a style that blends European and highland tradition, with a high roof and carved decoration inspired by the communal houses of the Bahnar people. It is still used for services, and the interior is cool, dark and handsome. Beside it, a small orphanage and a museum have been run by the church for many years. Around the outskirts, tall, steep-roofed communal houses stand in the minority villages, the centre of village life, and the carved beams and thatch are worth a visit.

This is also a landscape of war and memory. The Ho Chi Minh Road, the supply route that ran through the mountains along the border during the Vietnam War, passes through the highlands, and the modern highway follows part of it. North of Kon Tum, the area around Dak To saw some of the fiercest fighting of the conflict. Today the road is a peaceful, scenic route through forest, tea and coffee, with views of the Truong Son mountains in the distance. The ride from Phong Nha is long and varied, and arriving in Kon Tum after a day among hills and rubber trees is a good moment.

Fuel is easy, with a city of nearly fifty thousand people, and food is cheap and good, with local dishes such as grilled meat, bamboo shoots and rice wine. Coffee is a speciality, since the highlands produce much of Vietnam's crop, and cafes are on every corner. The climate is milder than the coast, with a rainy season from May to October, and mornings can be misty and cool. Take care on the road, where trucks, motorbikes and buffalo share the way, and avoid riding at night. A walk along the river at dusk is a fine way to finish.
t.teguise@29.1,-13.6:
Teguise was the capital of Lanzarote for more than four centuries, until the provincial government moved to the port of Arrecife in 1852, and it has the faded dignity of a city that remembers being important. The old town is a grid of whitewashed houses with green or blue shutters, small plazas and low churches, laid out on a plain in the interior of the island, away from the coast. The reason for the inland position was pirates. In the sixteenth century, raiders from North Africa and Europe regularly descended on the coast, and in 1586 the Algerian corsair Murat Reis sacked Teguise itself, so the island's rulers wisely kept their capital out of sight of the sea.

The name comes from Teguise, a native princess who, according to tradition, married the Norman conqueror Maciot de Béthencourt in the early fifteenth century. Her likeness appears in town sculptures, and her name is on a good many shop signs. Above the town, the Castillo de Santa Bárbara stands on the crater of the Guanapay volcano, a little fortress built in the sixteenth century to watch for pirates, and now holds a museum of piracy. The climb is short and the view across the plain to the coast is the best on the island.

Sunday morning is when Teguise comes alive. The weekly market fills the main square and the streets around it, with stalls selling crafts, jewellery, clothes, cheese, aloe vera products and plenty of things you do not need, and it draws visitors from all over the island. Arrive early or expect crowds and slow-moving traffic. On other days, the town is quiet, and the narrow lanes are a good place to walk and look at the architecture.

The roads around Teguise cross a wide plain of black volcanic soil dotted with palms, and they are gentle and open. The wind is constant, sometimes strong, and can catch a bike off guard on exposed sections. The surface is generally good, the traffic is moderate, and corners are mostly gentle. Hairpins appear only when the road climbs toward Haría and the northern cliffs. The island is sparse and dry, with stone walls protecting plants and strange, volcanic shapes in every direction.

Teguise has fuel stations, supermarkets and a decent selection of cafés and restaurants, so it is a sensible base. Local dishes include fresh fish, goat cheese and wrinkled potatoes with mojo, a salty garlic and chilli sauce. Visit on a weekday if you want peace, or Sunday if you want the market and do not mind sharing.
t.haria@29.1,-13.5:
Haría lies in a green valley in the north of Lanzarote, which is a surprise on an island that is mostly black and brown. The valley is full of palm trees, thousands of them, planted over centuries, so that from the hills above, the village looks like a settlement in a North African oasis. The whitewashed houses with flat roofs sit among the palms, and in the middle is a quiet square with a church and a few cafés. It is known as the Valley of a Thousand Palms, and the number is not far from the truth.

The village is also associated with César Manrique, the Lanzarote artist and architect who shaped the modern look of the island from the 1960s onward. He pushed for low, white buildings, no billboards and respect for the volcanic landscape, and the island's character owes a great deal to him. Manrique spent his last years in a house in Haría, which is now a museum and gives a good sense of how he lived and worked, with the typical mix of black lava, white walls and bright colour. On Saturday mornings, a craft market fills the village square.

For riders, the road from Teguise to Haría is one of the best on Lanzarote. It climbs gently across the plain, then curves up into the Famara massif, with sweeping views of the valley and the sea, and drops into the palm-filled basin of the village. The surface is generally good, corners are open and the traffic is light, though a procession of tour coaches heads for the viewpoint at Mirador del Río. Wind is a factor, particularly on the ridge, and fog can come in over the cliffs. Take it slowly, and look out for goats.

Haría has about five thousand inhabitants and a few shops, bars and restaurants, which are enough for a coffee or a lunch. For fuel, the safer option is Teguise, about eleven kilometres away, where there are stations and supermarkets. The surrounding landscape is farmed with stone walls and terraces, and the soil is covered with volcanic gravel that holds moisture, a method used for vines, figs and sweet potatoes, and the local cooking draws on these.

Early morning light on the valley, with the palms backlit and mist on the hills, is a good reason to start early.
t.mirador del rio@29.2,-13.5:
César Manrique built a viewpoint out of a cliff and made it look as though it had always been there. The Mirador del Río stands on the Risco de Famara, a sheer wall of rock about 475 metres above the sea at the northern end of Lanzarote, and it is half hidden in the hill, a low white building with a curved roof, and round windows that look over the water. From its terrace and glass windows, you see the narrow strait called El Río, the island of La Graciosa lying flat and pale in the blue, and the other small islands of the Chinijo archipelago beyond.

Manrique designed it in the early 1970s, on the site of an old military gun emplacement, and the building has become a symbol of his philosophy: make architecture serve the landscape rather than overwhelm it. The interior is all curved white walls and round windows, a quiet space with a café and a small shop, and from the outside it is almost invisible. The view is the thing. Below you, the salt pans of Salinas del Río glimmer in the strait, and on clear days the whole coastline of the north is spread beneath. An entrance fee is charged, and in high season there is often a queue.

The ride is a short and rewarding one. From Haría, the road climbs to the cliff top in a series of bends, with views opening on either side, and ends at a car park beside the building. The surface is good, the corners are well-marked, and the wind is usually strong. Cloud often settles over the cliff in the morning, and a view that was clear at nine can disappear by ten, so check conditions before committing.

A café at the viewpoint serves drinks and light snacks, with prices to match the view. From the coast road at Orzola, ferries cross to La Graciosa, if you want to add an excursion.

t.xian@34.3,108.9:

t.turka@52.9,108.2:

It is Buryat land, and you will see shamanic shrines, with poles wrapped in coloured ribbons, at passes and sacred places along the road. The light is clear and sharp, the sky enormous, and the wind can be ferocious. The sarma, a violent wind that pours out of a valley to the north, can whip the lake into dangerous waves in minutes.

As the start of a ride onto Olkhon, Sakhyurta sits at the end of a long road from Irkutsk, about two hundred and fifty kilometres through forest and then steppe. The final section winds over low hills, with long views of the lake ahead. The surface on the main road is paved, but watch for potholes and gravel on the edges. On the island itself, roads are mostly unpaved, sandy and rutted, with washboard surfaces that shake everything loose. Tyre pressures and a steady pace matter.

There are cafes, small shops and guesthouses at Sakhyurta, but fuel is limited. Yelantsy, about twenty-six kilometres back toward Irkutsk, has a station, and the smart move is to fill up there and carry extra, because fuel on Olkhon is not always available. The ferry is the next step, and the wait can be long in peak season. Use it to watch the water, the gulls and the island rising across the strait, and to feel the edge of the steppe meeting the lake.
t.olkhon ferry@53.0,106.7:
The crossing to Olkhon takes only a quarter of an hour or so, but the wait can stretch to several hours on a July weekend, when cars, minibuses and motorcycles queue along the road down to the landing. The strait here, known as the Olkhon Gate, is narrow, a couple of kilometres across, but deep and sometimes rough, and the small ferries that shuttle back and forth are a lifeline for the island. In winter, when the lake freezes, an ice road replaces them, and in the uncertain weeks of freeze-up and thaw, hovercraft take over.

Standing on the deck, you get one of the best views on the lake. To the north stretches the Maloye More, the Little Sea, between the island and the mainland, with bare hills and steppe on both sides. To the south, the main body of Baikal opens up, vast and blue, with mountains on the far shore. The island ahead looks dry and brown, with rocky headlands and patches of forest, and the air smells of water and wild thyme. Gulls follow the ferry, and on calm days the water is so clear you can see deep into it.

The ride to the ferry comes after a long road from Irkutsk through forest and the Tazheran steppe, the final stretch descending to the shore with views of the strait. On the island side, the road to Khuzhir, the main village, is unpaved, sandy and rutted, with long washboard sections that are tough on bikes and riders. Lower tyre pressures, a steady speed and plenty of patience help. Dust can be a serious problem in dry weather, so keep a distance from the vehicle ahead.

Services around the ferry landing are limited to cafes and small shops, with fuel back in Yelantsy, about thirty kilometres away. On the island, fuel can be scarce, so arrive with a full tank and extra if you plan to explore. Check the ferry schedule before setting out, especially in shoulder seasons, when crossings can be cancelled due to wind or ice. Then sit back, enjoy the crossing, and watch Olkhon come closer; there is something special about arriving on an island by water.
t.cape burkhan@53.2,107.3:
Shaman Rock rises from the water at the edge of Khuzhir like a pair of pale marble towers joined at the base, and for the Buryats it is one of the most sacred places in Asia. They call the cape Burkhan, after a deity said to live in a cave inside the rock, and for centuries shamans held rituals here, while ordinary people approached with caution, or not at all. Today the headland is crowded with visitors in summer, but the poles wrapped in coloured ribbons, the scattered offerings of coins and the sense of a place that matters to people are all still there.

The rock is made of marble and crystalline limestone, streaked with lichen in shades of orange and green, and it stands at the end of a short peninsula that juts into the Maloye More. The cave runs through it, and the views from the cape take in the water, the bare hills of the mainland across the strait, and the long sweep of sandy beach curving away to the north. At sunset the rock glows warm and golden, and the lake turns silver, which is when most photographers gather. In winter, the ice around the rock forms extraordinary shapes and icicles.

Khuzhir, the main village on Olkhon, is a dusty, sprawling place of wooden houses, guesthouses and cafes, with unpaved streets that turn to sand in summer and mud after rain. The ride from the ferry follows rough, sandy tracks across the island, with washboard sections and soft patches that demand care. Around Khuzhir, tracks lead north along the island toward Cape Khoboy at its tip, a rough, rewarding ride through steppe and forest with views of the lake on both sides.

Khuzhir has shops, cafes and plenty of guesthouses, but fuel can be hard to find on the island, so arrive with a full tank and spare. Try buuzy, the steamed meat dumplings of the Buryats, or smoked omul from the lake. Treat the rock with respect, as locals ask: do not climb it, and keep your voice down. Then find a spot on the cliffs nearby, watch the light fade over the water, and feel the quiet power of this place.

Egilsstaðir is the main town of east Iceland, set at the head of Lagarfljót, a long, dark glacial lake, with the Fljótsdalshérað plain spreading around it. For anyone riding the Ring Road around the island, it comes as a pleasant change after the empty highlands of the northeast, because suddenly there are trees. Iceland's largest forest, Hallormsstaðaskógur, grows along the lake's eastern shore, and the town has shops, a swimming pool and a handful of cafes.

The road here, Route 1, crosses the high plateau from Mývatn before descending into the valley, and it can be a harsh stretch. Wind is the main hazard. Gusts across the open ground can be strong enough to push a heavily loaded bike sideways, and fog and rain can reduce visibility quickly. Surfaces are generally good tarmac, but gravel sections and sudden changes can appear, and frost is possible outside summer. The best season for riding is roughly June to August, when the roads are clear and the days are very long.

Local legend adds a bit of colour. Lagarfljót is said to hold a serpent-like creature, the Lagarfljótsormur, and sightings have been reported for centuries. Whether you believe it or not, the lake has a calm, deep stillness that suits the story. From the town you can also drive toward the fjords to the east, with Seyðisfjörður, a steep-sided fjord with a ferry link to Europe, reached by a dramatic pass.

Fuel is not a concern here. Egilsstaðir, with its population of a couple of thousand, has stations, and the next ones toward the coast are at Reyðarfjörður and Eskifjörður, about thirty kilometres away, so fill up if you are heading to the fjords. In the empty stretches across the highlands, stations are far apart, so never let the tank fall below half.

This is a good place to rest, eat properly and check the forecast before the next leg. After the bare plateaus, the green valley and the calm lake feel almost gentle.

Haría lies in a green valley in the north of Lanzarote, which is a surprise on an island that is mostly black and brown. The valley is full of palm trees, thousands of them, planted over centuries, so that from the hills above, the village looks like a settlement in a North African oasis. The whitewashed houses with flat roofs sit among the palms, and in the middle is a quiet square with a church and a few cafés. It is known as the Valley of a Thousand Palms, and the number is not far from the truth.

The village is also associated with César Manrique, the Lanzarote artist and architect who shaped the modern look of the island from the 1960s onward. He pushed for low, white buildings, no billboards and respect for the volcanic landscape, and the island's character owes a great deal to him. Manrique spent his last years in a house in Haría, which is now a museum and gives a good sense of how he lived and worked, with the typical mix of black lava, white walls and bright colour. On Saturday mornings, a craft market fills the village square.

For riders, the road from Teguise to Haría is one of the best on Lanzarote. It climbs gently across the plain, then curves up into the Famara massif, with sweeping views of the valley and the sea, and drops into the palm-filled basin of the village. The surface is generally good, corners are open and the traffic is light, though a procession of tour coaches heads for the viewpoint at Mirador del Río. Wind is a factor, particularly on the ridge, and fog can come in over the cliffs. Take it slowly, and look out for goats.

Haría has about five thousand inhabitants and a few shops, bars and restaurants, which are enough for a coffee or a lunch. For fuel, the safer option is Teguise, about eleven kilometres away, where there are stations and supermarkets. The surrounding landscape is farmed with stone walls and terraces, and the soil is covered with volcanic gravel that holds moisture, a method used for vines, figs and sweet potatoes, and the local cooking draws on these.

Early morning light on the valley, with the palms backlit and mist on the hills, is a good reason to start early.
t.near yaiza@29.0,-13.8:
Yaiza is a village that looks as though someone scrubbed it, in the nicest possible way. The houses are white with green shutters, the streets are tidy, and the gardens are full of palms, flowers and succulents, in a landscape that is otherwise black, red and brown. It has won awards for being one of the loveliest villages in Spain, and it owes a good deal of that to the influence of César Manrique, who persuaded the island to keep its architecture simple. The village is quiet, with a church, a small square and a handful of restaurants, and it feels calm after the coast.

Yaiza lies at the edge of Timanfaya National Park, the Fire Mountains, where the great eruptions of 1730 to 1736 buried villages and poured lava across a quarter of the island. The landscape is lunar: black cones, rust-red slopes, fields of rough lava and a silence that feels strange. The park is protected, and you cannot ride in freely, but a bus tour runs along a marked road through the most dramatic parts, with demonstrations of the heat below the surface, where water poured into a hole erupts as steam. A restaurant uses the volcanic heat to grill chicken, which is a novelty, if not a haute cuisine experience.

The road from Yaiza to the north runs through La Geria, a wine region that makes no sense on paper: the vines grow in individual pits dug into the black volcanic ash, each surrounded by a small stone wall to shelter it from the wind, and the grape is the Malvasía, producing a dry or sweet white. The pattern of black craters and green vines is one of the most remarkable farming landscapes in Europe. Many bodegas offer tastings, though the rider must keep a clear head. Roads here are smooth, with gentle bends, and the traffic is light, though the wind can be strong.

For fuel, Yaiza's own pumps are small, so a safer plan is to fill the tank at Puerto del Carmen, about ten kilometres away, or in Arrecife before you set out. Camels carry tourists across the ash at a slow plod, and you may find yourself stuck behind a line of them. Late afternoon is the best time, with warm light turning the cones to copper. A plate of local goat stew and a glass of Malvasía under the palms is a fine way to end the day.
